I found the paper you're looking for! Here are the details:

**Title:** "Implicit Self-Regularization in Deep Neural Networks: Evidence from Random Matrix Theory and Implications for Learning"

**Authors:** Charles H. Martin and Michael W. Mahoney

**Publication:** Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR), Volume 22, Issue 165, Pages 1-73, 2021

**Summary:** The paper applies Random Matrix Theory (RMT) to analyze the weight matrices of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), including both production quality, pre-trained models such as AlexNet and Inception, and smaller models trained from scratch, such as LeNet5 and a miniature-AlexNet.

**Key Findings:** The empirical spectral density (ESD) of DNN layer matrices displays signatures of traditionally-regularized statistical models, even in the absence of exogenously specifying traditional forms of explicit regularization, such as Dropout or Weight Norm constraints. Additionally, the paper identifies a novel form of Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization, similar to the self-organization seen in the statistical physics of disordered systems.

The paper is available at: https://jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-410.html

I found the paper you're looking for. SIGMA: Scalable Spectral Insights for LLM Model Collapse (arXiv:2601.03385) is authored by Yi Gu, Lingyou Pang, Xiangkun Ye, Tianyu Wang, Jianyu Lin, Carey E. Priebe, and Alexander Aue.

The paper addresses "model collapse"—a degenerative process where recursive training on model-generated content leads to a contraction of distributional variance and representational quality. SIGMA is a framework that benchmarks model collapse through the spectral lens of the embedding Gram matrix, using deterministic and stochastic bounds on the matrix's spectrum to provide a mathematically grounded metric to track the contraction of the representation space.

The paper was submitted on January 6, 2026, with the most recent version (v3) dated March 23, 2026. You can access it directly at https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03385.

I found the paper! Here's what the search reveals about this work:

"Mind the Gap: a Spectral Analysis of Rank Collapse and Signal Propagation in Attention Layers" by Alireza Naderi, Thiziri Nait Saada, and Jared Tanner provides a detailed rigorous exploration of the challenges and mechanisms inherent in transformer architectures, particularly focusing on the self-attention layers predicated on softmax mechanisms.

**Key findings:**

The paper addresses three major issues in transformer attention layers:

1. Vanishing/exploding gradients and rank collapse in depth
2. Rank collapse in width, which occurs as the context length increases—a challenge unique to softmax attention layers

**Main contribution:**

Using Random Matrix Theory, the authors conduct a rigorous analysis that uncovers a spectral gap between the two largest singular values of the attention matrix as the cause of rank collapse in width, which in turn exacerbates the other issues. Building on this insight, they propose a novel yet simple practical solution to mitigate rank collapse in width by removing the outlier eigenvalue(s).

**Publication:**

The paper will be presented at the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), 13th - 19th July 2025, Vancouver, BC, Canada. The paper is also available on arXiv and has an associated GitHub repository with code.

I found the paper! Here are the search results for Muennighoff's "Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models" from NeurIPS 2023:

## Overview

The paper was authored by Niklas Muennighoff, Alexander Rush, Boaz Barak, Teven Le Scao, Nouamane Tazi, Aleksandra Piktus, Sampo Pyysalo, Thomas Wolf, and Colin A Raffel, and was published at Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023).

## Key Contributions

The paper addresses how language models scale when both parameter count and training dataset size increase, noting that training dataset size may soon be limited by the amount of text data available on the internet, motivating an investigation of scaling language models in data-constrained regimes.

The researchers ran a large set of experiments varying the extent of data repetition and compute budget, ranging up to 900 billion training tokens and 9 billion parameter models.

## Main Findings

They found that with constrained data for a fixed compute budget, training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data. The authors proposed and empirically validated a scaling law for compute optimality that accounts for the decreasing value of repeated tokens and excess parameters.

## Recognition

The paper received an Outstanding Main Track Paper award, Runner-Up at NeurIPS.

The paper is available on arXiv (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264) and through the NeurIPS proceedings.

Note: The search results show the author as Olivier Roy, not Roy Vetterli - Vetterli is the second author.

## Paper Overview

The mixture proportions of pretraining data domains (e.g., Wikipedia, books, web text) greatly affect language model performance. The paper proposes Domain Reweighting with Minimax Optimization (DoReMi), which first trains a small proxy model using group distributionally robust optimization (Group DRO) over domains to produce domain weights (mixture proportions) without knowledge of downstream tasks.

## Authors

The paper was authored by Sang Michael Xie and 9 other authors including Hieu Pham, Xuanyi Dong, Nan Du, Hanxiao Liu, Yifeng Lu, Percy Liang, Quoc V. Le, Tengyu Ma, and Adams Wei Yu.

## Key Results

The experiments use DoReMi on a 280M-parameter proxy model to set the domain weights for training an 8B-parameter model (30x larger) more efficiently. DoReMi improves average few-shot downstream accuracy by 6.5% points over a baseline model trained using The Pile's default domain weights and reaches the baseline accuracy with 2.6x fewer training steps.

## Publication

The paper was published at NeurIPS 2023 as a spotlight presentation.

You can find the full paper at the official NeurIPS proceedings and on arXiv (2305.10429), as well as a PyTorch implementation available on GitHub.

I found the paper! Here's what I found about this work:

**Paper Overview:**

The paper investigates why deep neural networks suffer from loss of plasticity in deep continual learning, failing to learn new tasks without reinitializing parameters.

**Key Finding:**

The authors show that this failure is preceded by Hessian spectral collapse at new-task initialization, where meaningful curvature directions vanish and gradient descent becomes ineffective. More specifically, spectral collapse is a degeneration of the Hessian eigenspectrum, indicating loss of curvature in most directions.

**Proposed Solutions:**

To characterize the necessary condition for successful training, they introduce the notion of τ-trainability and show that current plasticity preserving algorithms can be unified under this framework. Targeting spectral collapse directly, they discuss the Kronecker factored approximation of the Hessian, which motivates two regularization enhancements: maintaining high effective feature rank and applying L2 penalties.

**Results:**

Experiments on continual supervised and reinforcement learning tasks confirm that combining these two regularizers effectively preserves plasticity.

**Authors:** Naicheng He, Kaicheng Guo, Arjun Prakash, Saket Tiwari, Ruo Yu Tao, Tyrone Serapio, Amy Greenwald, and George Konidaris

The paper appears to have been presented at NeurIPS 2025.

I found the paper! Here's what I discovered about arXiv 2509.22335:

**Title:** Spectral Collapse Drives Loss of Plasticity in Deep Continual Learning

**Authors:** Naicheng He, Kaicheng Guo, Arjun Prakash, Saket Tiwari, Ruo Yu Tao, Tyrone Serapio, Amy Greenwald, George Konidaris

**Status:** The preprint was submitted on September 29, 2025 and is under review

**Main Research:** The paper investigates why deep neural networks suffer from loss of plasticity in deep continual learning, failing to learn new tasks without reinitializing parameters

**Key Findings:** The authors show that this failure is preceded by Hessian spectral collapse at new-task initialization, where meaningful curvature directions vanish and gradient descent becomes ineffective

**Approach:** They introduce the notion of τ-trainability to characterize successful training conditions and discuss the Kronecker factored approximation of the Hessian, which motivates two regularization enhancements: maintaining high effective feature rank and applying L2 penalties

**Results:** Experiments on continual supervised and reinforcement learning tasks confirm that combining these two regularizers effectively preserves plasticity
